label: Restlessness
framing: Restlessness is not always a problem to be solved. It is often the soul telling the truth, that it was made for more than it has found, and Scripture treats that ache not as a flaw to suppress but as a signpost pointing past every lesser rest.
cultural: Our age answers restlessness with the next purchase, the next screen, the next destination, promising that the cure is one more thing away. Scripture exposes the lie in the Preacher's verdict that all of it is vapor and a chasing after wind, and it redirects the hunger rather than feeding it, naming the one rest that does not run out.
historical: Augustine, in the late fourth century, gave the ache its most famous words, that God has made us for himself and our heart is restless until it rests in him. The Hebrew people carried the same lesson through forty years of wilderness wandering before the land, and the writer of Hebrews read that whole story as a parable of a rest still waiting for the people of God.
application: Stop expecting the next thing to settle you, and let the restlessness drive you toward God rather than away from him. Practice a real stillness, a Sabbath, a walk, an hour without a screen, long enough to hear what the noise has been covering. Ask whether the unease is the soul's true hunger or only an unwillingness to sit with yourself, since both wear the same face. And put your roots down somewhere, since restlessness often heals not by moving on but by staying put.

verses.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.
verses.where: After his poem of a time for everything, the Teacher says God has made everything beautiful in its time and has set eternity in the human heart, yet people cannot grasp the whole of God's work. The site's note on the chapter sets this beside the fourteen pairs of opposites that fill a life. The heart carries a longing that no single season of life can fill.

verses.text: Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my labor. Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
verses.where: The Teacher tests pleasure, wine and great projects, denying himself nothing his eyes desired, and when he looks at all he has done he finds it futile, a pursuit of the wind. The site's note says he ends the chapter recognizing that the simple ability to eat, drink and enjoy work comes from the hand of God. Getting everything did not settle him; receiving it from God was a different thing.

verses.text: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost! Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy? Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods.
verses.where: God calls everyone who is thirsty and has no money to come and eat for free, and asks why people spend their money on what is not bread and their labor on what does not satisfy. The site's note on the chapter says he offers an everlasting covenant and freely pardons those who return. The question is asked by the one who can actually feed them.

verses.text: Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again. But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.”
verses.where: At Jacob's well Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that whoever drinks that water will thirst again, but the water he gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. The site's plain note says she wanted water so she would not have to keep walking to the well, and that he does not mock the smaller request but keeps offering more than was asked: himself.

verses.text: O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water.
verses.where: In the dry wilderness of Judah, David says his soul thirsts for God and his body yearns for him in a weary land without water. The site's plain note says thirst is a sign of life, and that longing toward God is itself a kind of prayer. It notices that he is still in the desert when he says his soul is satisfied.

verses.text: “For My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns— broken cisterns that cannot hold water.
verses.where: The LORD says his people have committed two evils: they have forsaken him, the fountain of living water, and dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water. The site's note on the chapter says they traded him for worthless idols and ran after foreign powers for help. Much restless searching is digging, again and again, where water will not stay.

verses.text: There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His. Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience.
verses.where: The letter says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters God's rest rests from his own work, as God did. The site's note says the rest is received by faith and yet calls for effort, a paradox the author leaves standing. The plain note asks whether a person lives as one who has entered God's rest, or as one still trying to prove themselves.

verses.text: I am not saying this out of need, for I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances. I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. I am accustomed to any and every situation—to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need.
verses.where: Writing from prison, Paul says he has learned to be content in any circumstance, in being filled and being hungry, in plenty and in need. The site's plain note says the strength Christ gave him was the strength to be content. Contentment, in his own word, was learned.

verses.text: For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence— but you were not willing.”
verses.where: To a people rushing to Egypt for help, the LORD says that by repentance and rest they would be saved and their strength would lie in quiet confidence, but they were not willing. The site's note says the plan was made without asking his advice and rested their security on a foreign power. The chapter goes on to say the LORD longs to be gracious to them.

verses.text: All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own. If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.
verses.where: The people of faith confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, longing for a better country, and God was not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. The site's plain note says being strangers does not mean not caring about the places we live: Abraham dug wells and made peace with his neighbours. Some longing is for a home that is not finished yet.

misread.taken: There is no peace for the wicked is said of anyone who cannot settle, or quoted at a restless believer as if not being able to rest proved something was wrong with their soul.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says it is about Judah's idolatry, and that the same chapter has the high and holy God dwelling with the contrite and lowly and promising healing and peace to those far and near, while the wicked remain like a restless sea. The restlessness it names belongs to those who will not turn to God, and the chapter's answer is a promise to anyone who does. It is not a verdict on a person who cannot sit still or sleep.
misread.text: But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck. “There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked.”

whole: Restlessness takes many shapes. Changing jobs every couple of years, scrolling late into the night, starting projects and dropping them, needing the next trip or purchase to look forward to, never able to sit in a quiet room. Sometimes it is a vague sense that real life is happening somewhere else. Sometimes it follows a success: the thing a person worked for arrives, and within a week it no longer satisfies. Restlessness of the body that will not let a person sleep or sit still can also be a sign of anxiety or of an illness, and it is worth telling a doctor about.

Scripture treats much restlessness as a true signal aimed at the wrong things. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes denied himself nothing his eyes desired, and when he looked at all he had done he called it a pursuit of the wind. He also says God has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing within time can fill it. Jeremiah's picture for the same thing is digging cisterns: God's people left the fountain of living water and dug broken tanks that could not hold it. Isaiah asks why people spend their money on what is not bread and their labor on what does not satisfy. We are restless partly because we were made for more than anything we can get, and partly because we keep trying to get it from things that cannot give it. Scripture is honest that God's own people did this, and most of us will recognize ourselves.

So the Bible's wisdom is not to kill the longing but to take it to the right place. Jesus offered the woman at the well water that would become a spring within her, and Isaiah's invitation is to come without money and eat what is good. Paul says he learned to be content in plenty and in need; it was something he learned, not something he was born with. Isaiah told a people rushing to Egypt that their strength would lie in repentance and rest, in quiet confidence, and that they were not willing. It helps to notice what we reach for when we are restless and to bring the ache itself to God, as David did in the wilderness. And it helps to keep a rhythm of rest and worship, since the letter to the Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.

The hope Scripture gives is a homeland. The people of faith in Hebrews called themselves strangers and exiles, longing for a better country, and God was not ashamed to be called their God. Some restlessness will not be cured in this life, because it is a longing for a city that is not finished yet. That is no reason to despise the place you are in; Abraham dug wells and made peace with his neighbours. It is a reason to hold everything else more loosely, and to rest now in the one who has prepared that city.
deep.sit: What do you reach for when you feel restless, and what would it mean to bring the restlessness itself to God before you reach?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says this psalm asks you to practise setting the LORD always before you, on purpose, as a daily habit. Pray it when you wake, before your mind turns anywhere else.
prayer.text: I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely. For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.
